utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could -- if you want another copy we can get that after the break and take care of it. We have our copy of S3. Can we give that up? Yeah, we can give up our copy and we will submit another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So handing you, sir, for the record what has been marked as S3 a town map of Prijedor. We'll put that on the ELMO. And take a moment to orient yourself. And then if you could take the red marker, perhaps the big one will show up better, and just place an X where the petrol station was. Perhaps if the map could be moved up and to the right a little bit, and if we could focus down on the area of the river. Move it up a little bit, please. And perhaps we could closer up -- close in. Could we move the video in. Very good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The witness has drawn a circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, that would be just across the river from Stari Grad and from the Prijedor Hotel. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. A hundred metres or 150 metres as you cross the bridge on the right-hand side. So you don't have to take any other road, any side roads. The petrol station was on the main road, and I believe that the name of the street was Djuro Djakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Sir, who was your partner in that enterprise?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Slobodan Grahovac. He was the main partner because it was his company who took the lease. I said yesterday that I was his partner in that business.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Grahovac was a member of the SDS party. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who did you lease the petrol station from? Who was the actual owner?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not lease it. I just started working with him. I did not lease it. As far as I know, this petrol station was the property of INA Zagreb up to the year 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So no rent was paid as far as you know for this? You didn't pay any rent, you and your partner, to anyone?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did, of course we paid. We paid to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. That is, to the Executive Board. We paid the rent as far as I know. He had taken the lease earlier on. I don't know whether there was a bidding or not. I'm not familiar with that. But I just joined him. We made an agreement, and we started working together. He already leased it, and I know that he paid rent regularly to the Municipal Assembly. He paid a monthly rent. I know because I saw the financial accounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, what was your contribution? You didn't own the land. You said you didn't go and work at the station yourself. What was your contribution to this partnership?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I controlled the work of the petrol station. I was in charge of purchasing the oil derivatives. It was a complex activity, required a lot of travelling. And one man alone could not do it himself. There were long distances between the place where the raw material was and the petrol station. So I was in charge of the organisation of work to control the petrol station, drivers, the purchase of petrol, reports of all kinds. I had a lot of work to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The petrol station, do you know what -- when Mr. Grahovac began to lease this station and pay rent to the Municipal Assembly? When was it that he was given the right to operate that station?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The gentleman had another private petrol station. That was his own petrol station, and I really don't know when he leased this particular one. And let me just clarify one thing: I participated in a bidding for another petrol station, and let me explain it because it is very important. It is very important how the two of us forged this partnership. I participated in a bidding for a petrol station of Energopetrol, and I participated in that bidding. And that petrol station was the property of Energopetrol from the year 1960 or 1965, in Ljubija in my native village. I took that petrol station, and that's how I formed partnership with him. So we did not form partnership just like that. We joined the -- or merged the work of these two petrol stations. He had his means of transportation. I didn't have them. And that's how he helped me. And after a certain time, this is a very small petrol station in Ljubija, and we also paid -- I paid regular rent to Energopetrol. It was -- it is a very small petrol station, and it was not viable. And after a certain time, I returned that petrol station to Energopetrol, and it is still run by Energopetrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm going to concentrate now on the station in Tukovi. When was it that you became involved in the partnership with Mr. Grahovac? During what period of time were you involved as a partner with him in the running of that station?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Late 1992. In 1992, I can't remember the exact date when it all started. It lasted between 1992 and 1997. For five years we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And sir, so did this begin, this partnership, during the time that Dr. Stakic was the president of the municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Dr. Stakic had nothing whatsoever to do with our petrol stations. I formed partnership with Mr. Grahovac because I had this other petrol station. And from then on, we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, where did you obtain the fuel? You said you were in charge of purchasing the fuel. Where did the fuel come from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Pancevo, from Pirot, which is in the south of Serbia close to the border crossing called Gradina, some 15 kilometres away from that border crossing is Pirot, and I also obtained it from Novi Sad sometimes. It all depended on the situation and on the supply at various places. Pirot is about 900 kilometres away from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are all these places you mentioned in Serbia? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At that time, fuel was very difficult to obtain. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that you travelled abroad to several countries in order to make purchases. And I believe you named some of these countries. Was that again during 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992, 1993, 1994, I went to Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And I believe you mentioned Hungary and some other -- I believe you mentioned Germany. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, I didn't mention -- I mentioned Hungary as a place where I met with Mr. Popovic, and I also mentioned Hungary when I went to Croatia via Hungary. And then I, on that same occasion, went to Slovenia, and I cross to Croatia at Ilirska Bistrica. And when I went to Germany, I went to purchase raw materials for Hidraflex. I would go to Vienna, to Frankfurt. I can give you the names of the suppliers that I visited if you want me to. I can give you the name of the companies that I had contacts with in order to purchase production materials and raw materials. I was also in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During 1992, in order to get these products, both the fuel and the products you needed for Hidraflex to Prijedor, did you transport them through Serbia, through these locations that you mentioned in -- earlier, a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990 and 1991, I travelled until the war started in Croatia. Before that, we never went via Belgrade because Zagreb is 90 minutes away from our town, and then it is easy if you go via Slovenia, you can go to Austria. That's the route we used. Later on, after the year 1991, 1992, we used different routes via Serbia, all of them. In 1991, I was among the last who crossed the bridge in Jasenovac before the offensive. I experienced all sorts of abuse. I had some money on me. I had a lot of problems because of that. But I managed to deal with that on the spot. And after that, we had to take other routes. And the most common route was Republika Srpska, Serbia. In Serbia, we would go towards Bulgaria or we would go towards Subotica further on to Hungary. Very often I would meet with Mr. Popovic as I have already said, and the meetings took place in Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In order to recall how difficult it was to obtain fuel and how valuable petroleum was among other products at that time, is it correct that in 1992 the border to Croatia was impossible to cross commercially or very difficult and that in transporting goods through Serbia, from the 30th of May, 1992, there was a United Nations embargo against trade with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia except for food and humanitarian goods, so that the combination of the conflict and the international embargo imposed by the United Nations made fuel a product of extreme value and very difficult to obtain?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was difficult to obtain it. But we had fuel, and our petrol station was not the only petrol station in the republic or in the federation that had fuel. Some of that fuel was from Serbia, some of it from Sisak. Once I also had cisterns working for the United Nations and obtained that fuel from Sisak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You obtained fuel from the United Nations. Can you explain that? I didn't understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There were some commodity reserves of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and they asked for some cisterns that would take the fuel from Sisak in the territory of Croatia. And that was organised via Slavijatrans based in Petrinja, so that was a tanker -- a fuel tanker that was given to them. It was not a fuel that finally reached Republika Srpska. They just asked for the services of transport. They asked for a tanker, and they paid us for the transport of fuel from Sisak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This would be an appropriate time. I do have quite a few questions remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Same is true for the Judges. The trial stays adjourned half past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.57 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. I thought, Mr. Ostojic, you wanted to deliver a message on the witnesses to come for Thursday and Friday. Do you have any news about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We actually did call during the lunch break, Your Honour, but we have not confirmed that yet. So as soon as we hear, we will advise the Court accordingly, and the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question was just because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, please. You are ready to proceed? Mr. Koumjian, the floor is yours, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday on page 45 of the LiveNote, you talked about your attempts to go see the President Cehajic, and you said beginning on page -- line 20: "My attempts failed on some dozen occasions. Mr. Cehajic never saw me. It was his secretary who would always make excuses for Dr. Cehajic. She would say 'he's not here. He's in a meeting. He is with a delegation.'" On page 71 of yesterday's transcript, you talked about seeing Dr. Stakic in the newspaper Kozarski Vjesnik. Beginning on line 7, you said: "In our municipality, we have the Kozarski Vjesnik newspaper. Dr. Stakic once, when there was a formal or a ceremonial occasion, when a factory was being opened or a production floor, or maybe there was some humanitarian action, so holding the position that he was holding at the time, of course, he appeared as a representative of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor." My question is: Based on your experiences, sir, living in Prijedor, including interactions with Mr. -- Professor Cehajic and Dr. Stakic, would it be correct that the duties of the president of the Municipal Assembly would include representing the Municipal Assembly with delegations and with -- in public functions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would you agree that the principal representative of the municipality was the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Who represented the municipality more than the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in economic terms, that is in matters of business, it would be the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. And the president of the Municipal Assembly, I've already said that if there was a social function or a reception at the president's -- that is, the president. And as for life itself in a municipality, that is under the jurisdiction of the Executive Board of a Municipal Assembly, in our case, the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, on all of these occasions that you talked about where you saw Dr. Stakic in the newspaper, it was Dr. Stakic who was representing the assembly and not Dr. Kovacevic at formal occasions and public celebrations. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that there were Dr. Stakic and Dr. Kovacevic and whoever came after them. Before them, it was Mr. Cehajic. The president of the municipality and the president of the Executive Board, they would be invited both. That's what I know about it. It can happen, say, that the president of the municipality is asked about a holiday or something, to give an interview to the newspapers about the life in the town or preparations for wintertime or some campaign or other. That is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was it part of the duties of the president -- was it within his competence to comment publicly on issues concerning life in the town?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I was not a politician, that I was a self-employed entrepreneur. I wasn't the head of his office. I wasn't the mayor, the president of the municipality, or of the Executive Board, so how can I know their duties are? I know it was to the Executive Board in 1993, 1994, 1995, 1996 with regard to some problems in my enterprise. I never went to the president of the municipality to try to solve these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that Dr. Stakic's door was always open to businessmen like yourself. Were you saying that yesterday just in theory, or did you, in fact, you go to Dr. Stakic and he received you in his office?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The door was not open insofar as businessmen were concerned. The door was opened for me only [as interpreted]. But I don't consider myself a major businessman. I worked a lot. There were other prominent people who went to Dr. Stakic or to the Executive Board, so it depended on the nature of the business of what had to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise to my learned friend, but I think that the witness didn't say what was entered in the transcript regarding the open doors. So maybe my learned friend could ask him again for whom the doors were opened. We think that the witness said that the doors were not opened only for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I understood --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please repeat the question. Ask him to answer the impression that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I heard, is it correct that you said that the door was not open only for you? In other words, it was open for others, not just yourself. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct. The door was open for all people. One knows what the protocol is when you asked to be received by the mayor or the president of the Municipal -- Executive Board, the door was open to everybody. It wasn't that I was the only one who could go to the president or the Executive Board. Anyone who needed it could go to see them, but there was a procedure to be observed in a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me be concrete and precise. I'm asking now about the time when Dr. Stakic was the president of the municipality of the Municipal Assembly in 1992. Would it be correct, do you have any experiences to know that the door, his door, was always open? Did you try to see him or do you know of other people who went to see him and were received by Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went to see him two or three times perhaps, and I know other people who went to see him. Some of them. Some of them. I wasn't in the municipal hall. I didn't work there. So I can't know everybody who came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for Your Honours, I believe the reference to yesterday's testimony was page 63, line 3, regarding the door to the Municipal Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to move on to another topic. You indicate you have more knowledge of your own business affairs. As the -- would it be correct to call you the manager of the Hidraflex company, would that be the correct title?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy owner of the company. We also had a manager for technical affairs and head of our financial department. During a certain period of time, they were under me. I said yesterday that I visited the owner, Mr. Popovic, in Rijeka, so it wasn't those employees who went there. It wasn't they that were responsible to me. We organised production so far as we could do it considering the time. So I was a manager, an executive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, as an executive at Hidraflex, would it be correct your company aided and assisted the army in its operations and in preparing itself for combat?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I already said, the company was putting out high-pressure piping. And we lost a considerable share of the market. We had no communication with the army, what the army needed from our company because we were highly specialised. We were making the speedometers for vehicles. We didn't have any consumer goods in our product mix so that nobody could take it from us or ask us to give it to him if a citizen came. We also made metal cords, so people were buying those things from us. But we could not -- we wouldn't have been able to survive had we not charged for our services. So that I didn't give anything to the army and didn't ask for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you supply essential equipment for the army and for army vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask to have a letter distributed to the parties and the Court. I believe the Defence has a copy already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is there an extra copy for Dr. Stakic that Dr. Stakic can follow the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We would appreciate that, yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Ms. Karper has one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Prastalo, I believe you see on the ELMO next to you -- perhaps we have an extra copy the witness can -- it might be easier for him to have it on the table in front of him. We have a document. And for the record I'm going to identify it by the stamp number P0007964 through 7966, a three-page letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be provisional S399B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, first is it correct that it is a letter on Hidraflex stationery signed by you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And is it correct that you sent this letter or that the date that appears on it is the 4th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. But I have to go through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Certainly, but before I ask you any questions, I was going to ask you to read the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court or parties want the entire letter to be read. Perhaps we can start then with just the second paragraph. Can you just read that out loud, sir, the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we should start with the beginning, especially to whom it is sent and the subject and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary to read out the entire document, but at least this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, would it be correct, sir, that the addressee is the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. And perhaps you can read the addressee, and it will be translated more accurately than I could guess at it. Who did you send this letter to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly of the municipality of Prijedor, the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And can you read the subject line, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Complaint against a decision of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor number 02-111-388/92 of 26th November, 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir, would you now read out the second paragraph. Read it out loud slowly so that the interpreters can follow. But if you can please read slowly because they have to translate while you're speaking.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Namely, I've worked for PP Hidraflex from its establishment performing commercial affairs to this company, was founded in 1990, and in line with the effective regulations has been duly registered and entered in the Court register at the competent Court in Banja Luka. From its establishment to this day, this company has scored very noteworthy results in its operation and its product mix, and the quality of its products have gained it access to the markets of the former Yugoslavia. "Likewise, until the present day, this company has always met all its obligations toward the society and established good cooperation with the authorities. At the time when the war conflict broke out and after that, to the present day, this company has placed itself at the disposal of the army of the Republika Srpska and all the stocks of finished products and production materials which could be used for defence purposes have been given to the army. "It is very well-known that this company is the only company in the territory of Republika Srpska and also the Republic of Srpska Krajina manufacturing hydraulic hoses indispensable for the mechanisation of vehicles, military and civilian alike. We have succeeded to - in cooperation with the army and the elector [phoen] of Prijedor - provide also the necessary quantities of electric energy so we had hardly any interruptions in the production. I think that these are very important facts which needed to be kept in the account when taking the conclusion. I also wish --" No, this is the end of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. If you need to refer to the letter before answering my next question at time any, you may do so. Sir, I'll ask you now again, did your company supply essential equipment to the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'll explain it. This letter was written to the Executive Board which was to seize the factory, that is, this letter is to the Executive Board because there is no reason to write to the Executive Board, I mean, we were a company which was properly registered and was paying all its dues, and we were corresponding with them to defend our plant. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that the civilian companies cooperated throughout the war with the army and were essential for the war effort of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is true that there was cooperation, but they did not take anything from us. There was no need for them to take anything from us. We had high-pressure hoses. We had metal cords. That is, we were there at their disposal, and if they had any need to take anything, they would have taken it surely whether we liked it or not. But this letter which I received -- I mean which I wrote and which I signed personally was addressed to the Executive Board from which I was defending the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And in the second paragraph that you read out, did you tell the truth, is this true what you wrote in the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say that we gave anything. It says that we placed it at the disposal of the army of Republika Srpska. All stocks are of finished products and production materials which could be useful for defence purposes. I mean, they know, the army knows what we are manufacturing and they can take it if they want to, but they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer, what you wrote in the second paragraph is true. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that we put it at the disposal because all that you asked me before that, all the companies that were operational naturally had to be used for defence purposes. Therefore, the army could take what they needed, but there was no need for that. And this letter I personally wrote to the Executive Board or the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor because they wanted to seize from me -- I mean from me, who wanted to seize the plant and put it under the jurisdiction of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, the record of your testimony will speak for itself. I won't debate it with you. I want to move to another subject. On page 63, you talked about -- well, I'll read your answer beginning on line 14 -- well, I'll read the question on line 12. "Did Dr. Stakic ever talk to you about the purchase of fuel for sowing and for harvest, and how was that done?" And you answered: "Yes, since my business was also oil derivatives and at that time there was no cash, and at one point Dr. Stakic told me he would try and obtain fuel from the commodity reserves, and that that fuel would be used for sowing and for harvest. He asked me if I could help him and if we could do that without any commission or fee. This oil from commodity reserve was sold at 55 and 50 pfennigs a litre. One price was for sowing and the other was for harvesting. He put that proposal forward before the executive board. The executive board approved that. "We obtained the derivatives from the commodity reserves, and we distributed that oil at some places where it was very difficult for the population to obtain. We transported that oil by our own system. We did not consider that a lucrative business but we thought it was a good thing to do. We did that one year for the sowing and harvest season, and this was all thanks to Dr. Stakic who asked us to do that and who organised everything." Is it correct, then, that when it came to the distribution of fuel for the planting and harvesting of crops, it was Dr. Stakic who organised that distribution of fuel?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic didn't organise the distribution of fuel. Yesterday, I said that it was the Executive Board which did it. And the system was -- and I'll repeat that. But before that, I'll say that he inquired with us because we're engaged in this, I mean the sale of oil and oil derivatives. He asked if the Municipal Assembly managed to procure oil for sowing and harvesting, whether our petrol station could distribute it or perhaps take it to some villages further away from Prijedor so that people wouldn't have to spend the money coming to the petrol station for that fuel. What was the system. The Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly received from the republics commodity reserves certain quantities of oil, and it was given to us, and we distributed it to the people for whoever had a paper entitling him to that oil.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir, let me ask you one more time to reconcile your testimony today with what you said yesterday. You said today, in this answer you just gave on line 14: "Dr. Stakic didn't organise the distribution of fuel. Yesterday I said it was the Executive Board which did it." Beginning on page 63 yesterday you said, regarding Dr. Stakic on line 20: "He put that proposal before the Executive Board, the Executive Board approved that." And then you ended your answer on page 64, line 1 and 2: "And this was all thanks to Dr. Stakic who asked us to do that and who organised everything." So, sir, can you reconcile your answer today that Dr. Stakic didn't organise the distribution of fuel with what you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously we did not understand each other. I said that we worked, owing to Dr. Stakic, without any fee or commission when we distributed oil because in our normal business, we make money. But when we were distributing other people's oil, we did not charge any fee although we spent our electricity and although we spent our time. And Dr. Stakic asked us about the system. He never did it before. That's why he asked us. We told him what the procedure was. He told us where the oil would come from and what we did, we redistributed that oil to the end users. That's what I said yesterday, and I am repeating it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, my question is not focussed on you. Is it correct, then, that Dr. Stakic organised the distribution, put the decision before the Executive Board for their approval? Isn't that correct? I'm not asking what you did; I'm asking what Dr. Stakic did.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered already. Let me give you some more details. Mr. Stakic came to us before that, and he was very much interested in how oil could be distributed to the population for sowing and harvesting. I wasn't an employee of the Municipal Assembly. I didn't know how it went. Mr. Milosavljevic was in charge of the distribution of oil, and he was in charge of agriculture on behalf of the Municipal Assembly. I never said that Dr. Stakic distributed the oil. Mr. Stakic simply, before all these events took place, before the oil was distributed, asked me and Mr. Grahovac to see how this could be organised. Now, as to how they obtained oil, I don't know, but my obligation was to give money for all the vouchers that I received, and then the money was to be taken to the commodity reserves. I don't know how they organised it. But there was Mr. Milosavljevic who acted on behalf of the Municipal Assembly and was in charge of the agriculture in the territory. Now, what they did, how the decision was made, whether it was Dr. Stakic was the one who proposed things and put the proposal forth for voting, I don't know. I did everything later on with the Executive Board. It was Dr. Stakic who made initial inquiries about our tankers and whether we could do the technical part of the distribution. And I claim that the oil was distributed through regular channels regularly. There was no smuggling. Whoever had a piece of paper entitling them to a certain quantity of oil was given oil from that batch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another subject. Sir, did you see evidence in 1992, any time that year, that the police in Prijedor responded to the directions or orders or regulations issued by the civilian authorities, the Municipal Assembly and Executive Board? Did the police enforce those decisions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That could not happen in Prijedor. Whether this was supposed to be that way, that the police answers to the Municipal Assembly or to the president of the Municipal Assembly or to the Executive Board, I don't know. I know that they are supposed to cooperate. However, the person who was the head of the police was not cooperative. It was not possible to do it with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I'm going to refer you to -- refer the Court and Defence to page 43 of yesterday's transcript. You were talking then about your company being taken over, and you said, beginning on line 15: "The police came on the basis of the decision of the Executive Board or their conclusion. Their conclusion or decision issued by the Executive Board. Since I didn't want to take the first decision, then the police, the regular police, came to move me out of the company. Some seven or eight policemen came." So, sir, isn't it a fact that you had personal experience with the police from Prijedor enforcing decisions of the civilian government of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the group that came into power had already told me before that they would do it. I stand behind my statement. A little while ago, you said that I had given everything to the army. Had I given everything to the army, how would they have then sent the police to take everything from me? They came based on the decision of the Executive Board, and I told you who wrote that. It was Mr. Indzic. A director was already appointed for other people's company. So it was the Executive Board who gave the document to the police. It was not Mr. Dusan Kurnoga, but the Executive Board. And the police came, but they couldn't do anything. Now, whether they had cooperated or not, I don't know. The only thing I know is that the Executive Board issued an order to the police. What system was in place, I don't know. But the police came, seven or eight policemen came. They told me that they had to stand guard over the building. They told me the building is no longer yours, a new director has been appointed pursuant to a decision of the Executive Board, and that is the truth, and there's no other truth but that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, how did you -- sir, how did you travel from Prijedor to Ljubija? What was the route that you took?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's just one road from Prijedor to Ljubija. First I had to cross the bridge in Prijedor. Then I passed my petrol station. I drive towards Sanski Most for about a kilometre. There is a crossroads there, and on that crossroads, it says "Ljubija, 12 kilometres," and I take that road. I live in Gornja Ljubija in Toma Peric Street Number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That route goes through the Brdo area, through Hambarine. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, how far was your office in Ljubija, your company, from the Ljubija football stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean my house in Ljubija? I had a family house in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, I'm sorry. First, your house, and second the Hidraflex offices. Thank you very much. What were the distances of those two locations from the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My house, my family house in Ljubija, is about a kilometre to two kilometres, a kilometre and a half. 1500 metres from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And how far was your -- was the Hidraflex factory?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 17, 18, or approximately 20 kilometres, because Hidraflex was on the road to Banja Luka at the exit from the town on the road, on the main road from Novi Grad to Banja Luka, 2 kilometres away from the town on the right-hand side towards Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I had misunderstood something. Thank you. Sir, how far away was your home from the iron ore mines in the area called Redak? I'm speaking of your home in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 7 or 8 kilometres, or -- between 5 and 7 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How far was your home from Jakarina Kosa?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the extensive travel and business that you conducted in 1992 from June through September of 1992, did you travel through Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Let me just clarify: My house is at the far end of Ljubija. And further on, there's nothing but surrounding villages. And my house is some hundred metres from the main road, and I did not need to go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And on your business travels, I presume you went to Banja Luka at times, did you travel through Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kozarac was on the left-hand side. The village of Kozarac. And then Kozarusa. And when I took the main road from Prijedor to Banja Luka, I passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, as a person who lived in Prijedor and travelled around the municipality, you saw the destruction in Kozarac in areas surrounding Ljubija. You saw the churches and mosques in Prijedor destroyed. Isn't that true? In fact, isn't that true, you saw that virtually all the churches and mosques in the town and in areas like Kozarac and Stari Grad were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that some houses in Stari Grad had been destroyed. Yesterday I said that I saw that. I didn't enter Kozarac. I did not go to any mosques or churches even before the war, so I did not need to go into Kozarac. The village of Kozarac is 2 kilometres off the main road, and I never entered it. And as for Ljubija, let me tell you that nothing was burnt down in Ljubija as far as I know. Not a single building. To this very day, there is a church in Ljubija, there is one orthodox church and one Catholic church in Ljubija. Nothing has been touched. No -- neither any of the churches or any of the houses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Let me -- sir, sir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as for the houses, I did see the houses as much as I could from the car during the daylight. It was very rarely that I took that road, but I did. There were some houses that had been destroyed and burnt down, but that was in the area of Hambarine. But I would not -- I'm sorry that this happened because that is the road that I took when I went to school. And earlier on, I would take that road every day. But yesterday, I said that I don't know. Whoever launched the attack on the army, problems ensued, and nobody could influence that. I can even say that this was not just the other people or the -- another ethnic group. But even in my place in Ljubija, we were no experts. We were just normal people. Nobody in Ljubija attacked either the police or the army. We knew that these did their job, and the people who lived in Ljubija remained living there going to school, working there. And they worked on their land. Nobody ever touched them because there had been no incidents. In those places where there were incidents involving the army where soldiers were being killed on their return from the Slavonian front line, and I've already told you who did that. And later it turned out that what happened in Kurevo happened. There was some unit there. I don't know. I just heard, but what I saw I told you. I told you what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, let me clarify some things. Isn't it true that by the time the army began cleansing the Ljubija area, the policy was no longer to burn but to take over the houses and to give them to Serb refugees? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the policy was. I only know that in Ljubija, nobody ever attacked the army, in Ljubija. These are two different areas. One is Hambarine, and the other is Ljubija. Yesterday, I said that I used to come to Ljubija and to this very day, we know exactly who lives in Ljubija. There are refugees from Grahovo, Glamoc. There are refugees. I can't say that there are no refugees. There are people of different ethnic background who have remained living in Ljubija. When one puts Ljubija in the context of the overall situation in the Republic, I believe that the situation in Ljubija was really good. As far as I know, no single house was burnt down in Ljubija. I didn't go and visit all of them, so I cannot really say with 100 per cent certainty that they were all untouched and remained intact, but that's more or less what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that prominent persons from Ljubija, such as directors of the Ljubija mine company of Croatian, Muslim, and Bosniak nationality, were taken to camps, many of them killed, that the policemen that you talked about of non-Serbian, of Croatian and Bosniak ethnicity in Ljubija were separated for a while after the takeover of Prijedor were later arrested and taken to the camps and most of them killed? As a person who lived in this small town and followed events you told us, you were aware of this, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't follow the events on the case-by-case basis. I don't know all the people in the municipality. In Ljubija, as far as I know, there were no executives living there. Ljubija is a worker -- working-man village, and I don't know whether you're informed. The mine stopped operating some ten years ago. They were preparing a new mining site, and no directors lived in Ljubija. I don't know who it was from Ljubija that was killed or separated. There are still people living in Ljubija who were in lower managerial positions. And as for the higher executives, none of them lived in Ljubija as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How far was your apartment in Prijedor from the Keraterm facility?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I lived for a while in Cirkin Polje, and later on I lived in my sister's apartment in Pecani. In the first location, the distance was about 5 to 600 metres. And when I was in town, it was about 4 to 5 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you aware either by hearing yourself or from discussions with other people of a massacre that happened at the Keraterm facility in late July when people in the town heard shooting and automatic weapons fire for hours during the night?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. I didn't hear any shooting. I can't remember whether I was in Prijedor at that moment or whether I was staying with my parents in Ljubija. I didn't hear anything like that. I never entered any of the investigation centres. I didn't need to, nor was I interested in that. I never took anybody to any of the camps. I never took anybody out of any of these investigation centres. A lot of people came to my petrol station, and they would tell me that they went to the collection centres in order to go abroad, to find it easier to go abroad. But I personally had nothing whatsoever to do with the collection centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You were not interested in what was going on in the collection centres?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard that these were collection and investigation centres. In the investigation centres, people were asked questions about weapons, arms, about the war and what was going on. As for the collection centres, I heard that lists are made there featuring people who wanted to travel abroad. I've never been in any of these centres, nor did I ever talk to anybody who was there from those centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you hear of the massacre at Koricanske Stijene about a group of persons being taken from Prijedor escorted by Prijedor police, Prijedor reserve police and massacred on the cliff at Koricanske Stijene, over 200? Did you hear abou that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know where Koricanske Stijene is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, in your socialising with Dr. Stakic all the way up through 1997, did he ever express to you regrets for crimes that happened when he was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor and the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never discussed any crimes. I was not even aware that crimes were taking place. If anything like that had happened, we never talked about it. I was not interested in that. I thought then and I still think that in these investigation centres, people were interrogated and asked questions about the attacks on the army and the police and that in collection centres, people were just gathering in order to travel abroad. I know that some people asked me how one could go abroad, because they had heard that I travelled a lot. I personally never took anybody anywhere. I personally never arranged for anybody to travel anywhere. And the only thing that I did, as I've told you yesterday, I took a colleague of mine to my place where he spent the night, and on the following day, I took him to a place where there was some sort of an organisation. I don't know whether it was Caritas or some other organisation that transported people by buses to Novska. And that's where I took him, to that organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'll ask you the question again as concretely as possible, if you can answer yes or no, please do so. In your conversations, did Dr. Stakic ever express regret for crimes that occurred when he was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that we never talked about crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, may I ask you to correct me if I am wrong related to your place -- to the places where you lived. Is it correct that in 1990, you left -- or your family left to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Your parents remained in Gornja Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the usher, please, to present once again the map S3-1. If you could please be so kind and take the green marker, and then mark the place where you had your first apartment in Prijedor. Mark it with a 1, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And your second apartment. And may I immediately ask you, when did you move from the one to the other apartment approximately? This with a 2, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you then please mark with a 3 Keraterm building, the area of Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We come back to this map immediately. May I ask you, today I didn't understand your answer on LiveNote page 63, line 9. There you said: "Now, as to how they obtained oil, I don't know. But my obligation was to give money for all the vouchers that I received, and then the money was to be taken to the commodities reserves." What are these vouchers, these vouchers you had to give the monies for?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were certificates when people paid in cash for the oil derivative, 50 or 55 pfennigs for selling. That is, the republic subsidized the difference in price because, of course, the oil did not cost that. But we -- you didn't understand me quite when you said that I didn't know how they had come by the oil. You get the oil from commodity reserves for sowing and harvesting and things like that. And I was not the one who wrote letters to the commodity reserves and would receive answers from them. It was the Municipal Assembly who did it. And I knew a man who was in charge on behalf of the Municipal Assembly to do that so that I think the documents from, for instance, the cadastre, from the land register, they would establish how much land everybody had and then he would be entitled to so much fuel. The Municipal Assembly -- I mean the Executive Board had its rules saying how much oil you were entitled per unit of land, and then it would be distributed to neighbourhood communities, to local communities, and there were lists in the neighbourhood communities, and that is how the fuel intended for agriculture was distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, to be quite clear, I didn't ask you anything. I just quoted from your answer of today. Second, could you please name the person from the Municipal Assembly you had contact with. I just said "I knew a man who was in charge on behalf of the Municipal Assembly to do that so that I think the documents from, for instance, cadastres, the land register, they would establish how much land everybody..." and so on. Who was the man in charge on behalf of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ratko Milosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And why on behalf of the Municipal Assembly? You didn't hear the question, I take it from your gesture. Why on behalf of the Municipal Assembly, as you told us twice? What had the Municipal Assembly to do with this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again. We are talking at crosspurposes, the Executive Board. I call it that. Perhaps that was the reason. It was the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly was responsible for the fuel distribution, for the oil distribution, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. You need not repeat the answer you gave us. It's the same answer several times. But you always stated the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly. Would it then be correct that the Executive Board was part or under the control of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, I don't know how they are organised. All I know is that in the municipality, there are legislative and executive branches. And that is what the Executive Board did, and all it did was deal with economic matters. So that was organised by the Executive Board only. And the -- there were different sections attached to the Executive Board, and one of them was the section for agriculture, and it was headed by Mr. Ratko Milosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How often have you been in Prijedor since your family left to Belgrade in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite often. I cannot say long I would be absent per month, but I was in Prijedor, in Ljubija, I was away somewhere. Visited my family in Belgrade sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it once a week, two days a week you had been in Prijedor? Let us focus on the period of time 1992 as from April through September.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at times I would be away for seven days at a stretch. At times it would be two days travelling somewhere. So there was no rule. But I was spending more time in Prijedor than away from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This facilitates the understanding. You mentioned Dr. Stakic's door was always open. We discussed it already. May I ask, when you tried to contact Dr. Stakic following -- as from May 1992, did you enter immediately the building of the Municipal Assembly or did you first try to get an appointment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said how I met him, that it was by chance. But if you want to go, you have to make an appointment to announce that you're coming to the secretary of the president of the Municipal Assembly, to see if he's free. We cannot come and go as we please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be correct that the secretary would make an appointment when you asked for such a date with Dr. Stakic? Please answer, because your nodding is not reflected on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So when you entered the building of the Municipal Assembly, where was the office of Dr. Stakic, when being president of the Municipal Assembly, located?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the first floor in - how shall I say it - the middle of the building. You enter first the secretary's room, the door to the left, that is where the president of the assembly sat. And the door to the right, the vice-president. That's how it was for years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And let's take a concrete example. You mentioned today, transcript page 55, line 6, at about two or three times, it was at this period of time that you visited Dr. Stakic. When you arrived, you had first to enter the office of the secretary. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Who was this person?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a lady, middle-aged. I wouldn't really know her name. I think Milica, or Mila. But she was his secretary. I think that his secretary's name is Milica. I'm not quite sure, but I think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand. Did you make reference to a previous phone call reminding her or telling her that you had an appointment with Dr. Stakic, that she was sure that you were a person having in fact an appointment with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would call her to make an appointment. There was no need to check it, because she had it written down. And it was hers to check and tell us whether we could come or not. She was the one responsible for that because I can't know when the president is in the building or out of the building, whether he has a meeting or not. It's his secretary who knows such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be correct that his secretary had a book where she had scheduling order or where all the appointments were noted down?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, I don't know what she had when they talk over the phone. I dialed the number. She answers. And we asked for a meeting. And that's it. I don't know what she kept. Whether she kept a diary or just a sheet of paper for every day, how can I know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Maybe, as it would be usual, it could be, I don't know what happened, therefore I have to ask you. When you ask for an appointment, did she, for example, tell you, No, it's not possible. We just can see Dr. Stakic has already an appointment for this period of time. Did this happen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it did happen, yes. He's busy. Somebody's coming to see him or he's away. He's not in the building, which is only natural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you arrived, and following the appointment, did you see her crossing out your name on a calendar or scheduling order?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I had to wait, I would have a glass of fruit juice or a cup of coffee or something, if I had to wait at that room with her, unless -- until he would be free. But I didn't look to see whether she crossed out something, whether she crossed out something or put something in. She didn't fill in anything in front of me. The same rules applied to the Executive Board. That was the second floor, and again a secretary and again you call to make an appointment. You come, yes, he can see you. No, he can't. Then you wait. I mean, it was just the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Are you quite sure that the Executive Board was the second floor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a floor above, a floor above the office of the president of the Municipal Assembly. Perhaps a little bit more to the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it would be your testimony as you sit here that the president of the Executive Board and his deputy had not his office on the same floor as Dr. Stakic and his deputy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I went there, and I did, I would go to the upper floor, and there was also a secretary there. And again, I think if you had these same kind of the ground plan that there would be to the left would be the president, and to the right would be the vice-president. Now, whether I -- no, I don't think I did. I don't think I got them mixed up. No, I think I'm right. Or perhaps at that particular moment, when I was there, because they were painting the building for a while, putting the building in order. I don't know. But I was up there. Some of the offices in the Municipal Assembly were being painted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You had been there two or three times during the entire period of the presidency of Dr. Stakic, or maybe I'm confused. I have to go back to your testimony not to quote you incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You said page 55, line 6: "Well, I went to see him two or three times perhaps, and I know other people who went to see him." In which period of time was this, this two or three times, the entire year of 1992 or the period between, say, April and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, no. Two or three times, well, let's say three times to see him all together. But I did go to the Municipal Assembly more often because I went to the Executive Board. I didn't go there only to see the president of the assembly. I also went to the Executive Board. I also went to the secretary for economy. I went to see Mr. Milosavljevic for agriculture. I mean, it's not that I was in the municipal hall two or three times. I have been there more times but visiting different people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Based on your previous testimony, you gave the impression of a person who really knows how to act, how to react, and how to address the correct persons who are in charge of concrete areas, be it in the economic, be it in the political field. For example, the provisional-marked exhibit S399B, the letter of Hidraflex addressed to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, and then -Executive Board-. Whenever you had such a problem, and apparently you had at that time some problems with the bureaucracy, as it is always in the world, who would you contact first? When, for example, it was a question of expropriation was at stake, as you mentioned beforehand, whom would you contact first in 1992? I know the situation has changed since then.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I used the normal route. That is, the Executive Board, the executive branch, which was to do something. If I was to pay my taxes, if I didn't do that, then the Executive Board would order the financial police to come. So I first reported to the Executive Board, and I went to see the Executive Board except that the Executive Board turned a deaf ear on the private initiative. And there were all sorts of problems. I've already said what problems those were. And it was difficult to change a system and start another system, to have an assembly-employed person and to meet somebody who will show understanding for that. At that time it was very difficult in our case because some people who had come to hold certain offices, they thought that that was it, that was the high point of their career and that was that. But I was never a politician, I was never a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When your attempts failed on this level, to whom -- whom would you contact then to get assistance?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to establish contact with somebody else in some other office, if he could help me. If not, then I would continue further up to the republican level if need be. But let me tell you, during that struggle that I waged, I also paid other newspapers to write something so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll come back to this at a later point in time. Within Prijedor, when you had problems with bureaucrats in the area of the Executive Board, what was the hierarchy? It would be quite normal, and you are apparently a strong person, to whom would you go when your attempt to receive the one or other assistance, who would be the next superior? I'm always discussing now 1992 only, after the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you something: Unfortunately, and it is much to my regret that that is so, the president of the Municipal Assembly could not resolve anything in my case. Not the first one, not the second one, nor the third one because that is the rule with us. The executive branch regrettably assumed the right to be at the legislative authority, whereas the legislative branch couldn't do anything. So the president of the assembly, it would -- perhaps a friend who was not in the government could perhaps help me more if he knew some people on the Executive Board. Such a friend could perhaps help me more than ex officio the president of the Municipal Assembly. Why that is so, I do not know, but that is how it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What do you understand when using the term "government"? Who is the government in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean -- well, I look at it graphically. I look at the municipal hall and I say: "Well, those people in power won't let us do this or that." So when I say "government" and people who can take a decision and I cannot take a decision. So they are in a way people who are in power. They are the authorities. And -- all of the businesses in Prijedor, it wasn't only my company, it was everything, that was all accountable to the Executive Board. So be it myself, or be it the iron ore mine, they will apply with whatever requests to the Executive Board. Nobody would go to the president of the Municipal Assembly. You will go to the president, I repeat, to invite him to a social event, to add to the celebration. That is how it has always been with us, and I believe it's like that today. The president of the Municipal Assembly, the municipal mayor, can make suggestions, can talk with his colleagues, but they need not follow his advice. They can do that, but are not duty-bound to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please answer the following question with a clear yes or no: Did you ever go to Dr. Stakic complaining about the work of bureaucrats in the building of the Municipal Assembly, for example, those ones working with the Executive Board? Did you ever complain about their work with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dr. Stakic in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When have you been the first time in the office of Dr. Stakic after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days later, two or three. Less than five. I can't remember exactly, but I did go. I didn't stay long, a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you go to the Municipal Assembly after you -- immediately after the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not immediately. You mean the 21st, 22nd. No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not immediately. That would mean how many days later?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After what date? After --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: After 20 to 22nd of May, as you mentioned yourself.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, again, five, six, or seven days later. I didn't pay too much attention to that detail. I didn't consider it important. I went to see him two or three times all together. I visited the offices of the Executive Board more often than that. Sometimes they would invite me. Sometimes I would ask for an appointment with somebody from the Executive Board. It was not very much in line of my business to see the president of the Municipal Assembly. I had more to do with the Executive Board. That's why I went there more often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you see by the end of May people of the Executive Board wearing uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know all the people in the Executive Board. I told you whom I knew. I saw Dr. Travar wearing civilian clothes, Mr. Ranko Travar, that is. I also saw Slavko Budimir in civilian clothes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Would you please be so kind and answer my question. The question was: Did you see by the end of May people of the Executive Board wearing uniform? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you see the end of May 1992 Dr. Stakic wearing a uniform and a pistol?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. If he had worn a uniform, maybe I wasn't in Prijedor at the time to see him. I didn't see him. When we saw each other in town, he wore a suit and a tie. On weekends, he would wear a track suit. I never saw him wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A last attempt the other way around: Did you see when entering the building of the Municipal Assembly people wearing uniforms at all in the entire building?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. There were all sorts of people entering the building. There were army members, police members. I don't know all the people who worked in the Municipal Assembly, but there were people entering the building wearing uniforms. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Apparently one has to be more concrete. Did you see and meet persons you previously saw in civil clothing now wearing uniforms? Civil servants working in this municipal building.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: People who worked there and whom I knew, I didn't know all of them. I did know some people. But all of all those that I knew, I didn't see any of them wearing uniforms. But let me tell you again, I didn't work in the Municipal Assembly. I would only go there for half an hour, and then I would go back to my own work or I would go away on business. I wasn't there all the time. I saw people in civilian clothes, but I also saw people wearing uniforms who entered the building. Whether they worked there or not, I don't know. As for the people who were in power in the Municipal Assembly, Dr. Stakic and members of the Executive Board, those whom I knew, I didn't know everybody in the Executive Board. Those wore civilian clothes. They came to their offices wearing civilian clothes. That's as much as I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until half past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The usher may escort the witness in. The same question in your direction as usual, any news from your investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, we have called but we have not received any news confirming it. We called again both to our case manager and our investigator in the field. We just don't have any definitive news, so I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In case, you know my phone number, and you know my e-mail address. Please, let me know. I'll be here until 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll call you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear from the Prosecution, is there a delegation to be expected tomorrow or on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: To be frank, I'm a little confused. I believe there's a possibility Ms. Korner will be here tomorrow. Ms. Sutherland spoke to her. There -- I also had heard that the Prosecutor was requesting to speak to the Court on Thursday morning. She's not here tomorrow, Ms. Del ponte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So if we could get a final answer by the end of the day or by phone or by e-mail later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, we understood that Ms. Sutherland was going to speak to Mr. Johnson after Court. So we can -- perhaps not in Court, but we can call the Defence and Your Honours and tell you the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be nice. Thank you. Sorry, we had to discuss the one or other issue. Let's now continue with our line of questions. How often did you meet Dr. Stakic in his own home?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Prijedor, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I want to refrain from comments. In Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Omarska, I was there once. It was his patron saint's holiday, actually, his father's patron saint's holiday. That's where I was. But I was never in his apartment in Omarska. I only know that he rented an apartment in Omarska, and I was in Maricka only once in his father's house, and that was on the day when his father celebrated his patron saint's day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I have a two-fold answer before me. "In Omarska I was there once, and then I was in Maricka only." Have you been -- to be quite concrete, have you ever been in the apartment or the house - I don't know - of Dr. Stakic in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So as I understood, in his father's house. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you meet the family of Dr. Stakic there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you please tell me who are the members of the family you met there, please, by name.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: His father, his mother, his brother, his sister-in-law, Mr. Stakic. His father's name is Milan. His wife's name is Bozana. His children. Neighbours who were there, some of their relatives were there. When there is a celebration of the patron saints, then people are invited. Relatives, acquaintances are invited to come to the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I know about this custom. I have myself participated in such events in Berlin as well. But you mentioned nearly all the names, and you mentioned in addition that also Dr. Stakic's brother was there. What was the name of Dr. Stakic's brother?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him well, but I can't remember his name. I only know his nickname, his nickname was Baco. That's all I know. We are not that close. And I don't have to remember all the names in his family. This guy's nickname was Baco. Everybody called him that. That's how I called him as well. That's the name I knew him under.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't know why you emphasised that you don't have to remember all the names in a family. I only asked you whether you knew the names of all the other members of the family. Yes. You mentioned that you would know where Baco is living.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere in Prijedor. I also think that he rents an apartment there. I was never in his apartment, in Dr. Stakic's brother's house. I was never there. I know that he rents an apartment from a private landlord, but I've never been to his apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was he employed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had a workshop or a store selling electrical goods. It was a retail store actually in Prijedor. And I also heard in a conversation from him that he used to drive a lorry, that he was a hauler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you remember exactly that it was the -- a special day. Do you recall the year, only if you know, please. Was it in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in 1993. In 1993, it was, but I can't remember the month. But I'm sure that the year was 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was this the only time you saw the family or members of the family of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And later?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes I would meet his closest members of the family downtown. And as I've already told you, I quite often played billiards with Dr. Stakic and his son. And I also saw him -- as I was driving my car, I would see him or his wife bringing the child home from the kindergarten. That's when I saw members of his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you didn't socialise with other members of the family; you never had any additional meetings, be it in, to be quite concrete, be it in Prijedor, be it in Omarska, be it in Maricka, be it in Ljubija, be it in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other members of the family, I didn't understand the question. Are you asking me about whether I socialised with other members of his family? The answer is no, I didn't need to. I didn't socialise with any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And did you ever have meetings in one of these locations with other members of the family when you, for example, met Dr. Stakic, was he ever accompanied by another person? You mentioned this one special meeting, and then in addition the occasions when you played with Dr. Stakic's son together billiards. Were there any other occasions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PRASTALO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I didn't find it that important at the time. I told you when I saw them, where I was when I saw them. To my mind, it wasn't that important. I didn't pay that much attention to the occasions when I actually saw them because I didn't socialise that intensely with them. I've already told you that I spent a lot of time in Ljubija with my parents when I didn't have things to do in Prijedor. So I didn't spent all that much time with the family of Dr. Stakic. I held Dr. Stakic in high esteem because we shared the same opinion of business matters. But that doesn't mean that I socialised very intensively with his family. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now come to another area. In yesterday's transcript, page 51, line 4, when asked, you mentioned, quote: "I heard there was a Crisis Staff and that they were distributing vouchers for petrol, for flour."
